## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Uddālakajātaka* (Ja 487) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the story was told by the Buddha concerning a dishonest monk who engaged in a threefold practice of knavery in order to obtain the requisites of life [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta was the royal chaplain under King Brahmadatta; he fathered a child with a courtesan in a royal park, and because the boy could not bear the father's name, he was named Uddālaka after the tree under which he was conceived, receiving a ring to establish paternity [Sujato 2011]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the deceitful ascetic is identified as the dishonest monk in the present, the king as Ānanda, and the Bodhisatta chaplain as the Buddha [Fausböll 1887]. The text's opening verse begins with the incipit *Kharājinā jaṭilā paṅkadantā* [Fausböll 1887].

SuttaCentral notes the *Setaketujātaka* (Ja 377) as an established parallel [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates this relationship through Pali-internal text reuse, identifying a matching segment between Ja 487 (§0.4–4.4) and Ja 377 (§3.1–6.4) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus records substantial textual overlap with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (volumes 3 and 4), as well as automatic cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the Tibetan *aṣṭādaśapaṭalavistaravyākhyā*, and the Chinese *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100) [DharmaNexus].
